title: Reduced motion
learningObjectives: Explain reduced motion and apply it to accessible, reliable web development.

understand.concept: The prefers-reduced-motion media feature detects a user preference to reduce non-essential motion. CSS and JavaScript should avoid or simplify unnecessary movement while preserving content and interaction feedback.
understand.whyItMatters: Motion can cause discomfort or distraction. Respecting the preference makes the interface more comfortable without hiding essential information.
understand.analogy: A reduced-motion preference asks the interface to present the same information with less movement.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is simplified; web protocols, browser behaviour, and accessibility requirements follow formal standards and platform implementations.

explain.narrative: The hover movement is removed when reduced motion is requested; the content remains visible and usable.

examples.explanation: The hover movement is removed when reduced motion is requested; the content remains visible and usable.
examples.expectedOutput: The example illustrates the concept; some browser examples require a real served page and supported APIs.

practise.guidedTask: Audit animations on a lesson page. Add a reduced-motion alternative and verify that essential state changes remain perceivable.
practise.independentTask: Apply the concept to a small web page. Record the expected behaviour, how you tested it, and any limitations or fallbacks.
hints: Use browser developer tools to inspect actual behaviour.
Test with keyboard and different viewport sizes.
Keep core content available when enhancements are unsupported.

questions.prompt: What is a reliable web engineering habit?
options: Test actual browser behaviour and provide accessible fallbacks
Assume the browser always behaves exactly as expected

questions.explanation: Reliable web work combines standards knowledge with real testing and inclusive fallbacks.
